read.sections.0.heading.source: Start with what you can see

read.sections.0.text.note: Back-translation check: Fixed the awkward last sentence ('apa maksud karya seni itu yang mungkin') and the missing 'ialah' in 'Ia fakta'. Please check that it reads naturally.
read.sections.0.text.back: When you look at an artwork, start with what you see. Name the colours, people, objects and any words. Pay attention to the composition, that is, the way each of its parts is arranged. In this poster, a blue river flows through the middle part. Three people carry buckets towards one water tap, and a child points towards a cracked pipe. These are observations. They are facts that anyone can check by looking. The words “Water for every street” are also part of the evidence. Only after you have looked carefully do you then decide what the possible meaning of the artwork is.
read.sections.0.text.source: When you look at an artwork, begin with what you can see. Name the colours, people, objects and any words. Notice the composition, which means how the parts are arranged. In the poster, a blue river runs through the centre. Three people carry buckets towards one tap, and a child points at a cracked pipe. These are observations. They are facts that anyone can check by looking. The words “Water for every street” are also part of the evidence. Only after you look closely should you decide what the artwork might mean.

read.sections.1.heading.back: Art has long been used to tell stories
read.sections.1.heading.source: Art has told stories for a very long time

read.sections.1.text.note: Translator: The scroll's title is kept in English as a work name. It is sometimes known in Malay as 'Di Sepanjang Sungai Semasa Perayaan Qingming'. Check whether to keep the English title. Back-translation check: Translator flag stands: whether to keep the scroll's English title or use a Malay one. 'mengembara' (to wander, go on long journeys) is odd for people moving about a city. Consider 'dalam perjalanan' or 'bergerak ke sana sini'. The same verb is in the simpler text. 'pelukis pasir' for 'sand drawers': please check.
read.sections.1.text.back: People all over the world use art to tell stories and to keep knowledge. At Tassili n'Ajjer in Algeria, rock art shows hippopotamuses and herds of cattle. The land there is now desert, so the paintings tell us that the Sahara was once much greener. In China, there is a painted scroll that is more than five metres long. The scroll shows more than 800 people shopping, travelling and working in a busy city about 900 years ago. Its name is Along the River During the Qingming Festival. In Vanuatu, in the Pacific, sand painters use one finger to draw one long line. Their drawings help people remember stories and knowledge.
read.sections.1.text.source: People around the world use art to tell stories and keep knowledge. At Tassili n'Ajjer in Algeria, rock art shows hippos and herds of cattle. The land there is desert today, so the pictures tell us the Sahara was once much greener. In China, there is a painted scroll more than five metres long. It shows over 800 people shopping, travelling and working in a busy city about 900 years ago. It is called Along the River During the Qingming Festival. In Vanuatu, in the Pacific, sand drawers use one finger to draw one long line. Their drawings help people remember stories and knowledge.

read.sections.1.simpler.note: Back-translation check: 'mengembara' for 'travel' inside a city may sound odd. See the note on the standard text.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: People all over the world tell stories through art. In Algeria, old rock art shows cattle and river animals. Now that land is desert. So, the art tells us the land was once green. In China, a long painted scroll shows a busy city. It shows more than 800 people. They shop, work and travel. In Vanuatu, people draw on sand with one finger. The drawings help them remember stories.
read.sections.1.simpler.source: People all over the world tell stories with art. In Algeria, old rock art shows cows and river animals. Now the land is desert. So the art tells us the land was once green. In China, a long painted scroll shows a busy city. It shows more than 800 people. They shop, work and travel. In Vanuatu, people draw in the sand with one finger. The drawings help them remember stories.

read.sections.2.text.note: Translator: 'may' / 'might' are rendered as “mungkin” / “barangkali” (also used in write.selfCheck.1 and the simpler text). Check that this pair sounds natural as two hedging words. Back-translation check: Translator flag stands: check that 'mungkin' and 'barangkali' work as the pair for 'may' and 'might'. 'pelukis' (painter) is used for 'artist' here and in several other strings. Check that it is acceptable for a poster maker; 'artis' would suggest a performer. 'orang yang ingin dicapai' is a little stiff.
read.sections.2.text.back: An interpretation is an idea about the meaning of an artwork. A strong interpretation points to details. Viewer 1 is of the opinion that the poster is about people who do not have enough water. The line of people at one tap and the words at the bottom part support this idea. Viewer 2 is of the opinion that the poster is asking the city authorities to repair the pipe, because the child points right at it. Both ideas use evidence, so both can make sense. It also helps if you think about the audience, that is, the people the painter wants to reach. Words like “maybe” and “perhaps” show that you are being careful.
read.sections.2.text.source: An interpretation is an idea about what an artwork means. A strong interpretation points to details. Viewer 1 thinks the poster is about people who do not have enough water. The line of people at one tap and the words at the bottom support this idea. Viewer 2 thinks the poster asks the town to fix the pipe, because the child points right at it. Both ideas use evidence, so both can make sense. It also helps to think about the audience, the people the artist wanted to reach. Words like “may” and “might” show that you are being careful.

read.sections.2.simpler.note: Back-translation check: 'Siapa yang pelukis mahu capai?' may sound awkward. Check the phrasing.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: An interpretation is an idea about the meaning of a piece of art. A good interpretation points to details. Viewer 1 feels some people do not have enough water. Many people are waiting at one tap. That is a clue. Viewer 2 feels the poster is asking the city authorities to repair the pipe. The child points towards it. Both ideas use evidence. Think also about the audience. Who does the painter want to reach? Use words like “maybe” and “perhaps”.
read.sections.2.simpler.source: An interpretation is an idea about what art means. A good one points to details. Viewer 1 thinks some people do not have enough water. Many people wait at one tap. That is a clue. Viewer 2 thinks the poster asks the town to fix the pipe. The child points at it. Both ideas use evidence. Think about the audience too. Who did the artist want to reach? Use words like “may” and “might”.

write.example.back: This poster shows three people carrying buckets to one water tap. I also see a child pointing towards a cracked pipe. This might suggest that some streets do not have enough water. I think this because many people share one tap, and the words say “Water for every street”. watch.summary.back: This is the same short video from Lesson 15. This video comes from the Ayala Museum in the Philippines. This time, pay close attention to its details. The video shows a small green jar from China with two dragons on it. It shows a salakot, that is, a wide woven hat, decorated with shells and silver. It also shows a small piece of cloth sewn with a poem. Each detail is a clue. The dragons make the jar unusual, because most jars like it are not decorated. The shells and silver suggest that the hat belonged to an important person. The poem tells us the feelings of the cloth's owner. A careful viewer first states what he or she sees. Then, he or she states what its possible meaning is, and which details support that idea.
watch.summary.source: This is the same short video from Lesson 15. It comes from the Ayala Museum in the Philippines. This time, watch closely for details. The video shows a small green pot from China with two dragons on it. It shows a salakot, a wide woven hat, decorated with shell and silver. It also shows a small cloth with a poem sewn into it. Each detail is a clue. The dragons make the pot unusual, because most pots like it were plain. The shell and silver suggest that an important person owned the hat. The poem tells us how the cloth's owner felt. A careful viewer first says what they see. Then they say what it might mean, and which details support that idea.
